hero.headline: Florida insurance co-pay accumulator policy blocks Port St. Lucie man from cancer drug
hero.teaser: Mark Armstrong of Port St. Lucie cannot continue using a life-changing cancer medication because of his insurer's co-pay accumulator policy.
hero.body:
Mark Armstrong, who has battled the rare blood cancer polycythemia vera for years, experienced dramatic improvement after his doctor prescribed Jakafi, a newer but expensive treatment. Armstrong said by the end of the month he was feeling great, with reduced swelling in his legs, bearable headaches, and improved skin condition. His hematologist was amazed by the results. Armstrong's previous daily oral chemotherapy drug had become very toxic, causing severe side effects including major headaches, fatigue, skin ulcers, and splenic attacks.

Armstrong cannot keep using Jakafi because of a co-pay accumulator policy from his insurer, Oscar Health. Drug companies often help patients pay for expensive medications, but under a co-pay accumulator policy, insurers do not count that manufacturer assistance toward a patient's deductible. In Armstrong's case, the drug maker paid nearly $9,000 for his first prescription. When he tried to refill it, Oscar Health said he still owed his $7,700 deductible. Armstrong said he did not understand how the insurer could accept $8,600 from a manufacturer and still tell him he owed $7,700. The Armstrongs explained that if the money had come from a family member instead of the drug manufacturer, there would have been no problem.

Co-pay accumulators are so controversial that half of states in the United States have already banned them, according to a recent investigation by KFF Health News. Florida is not one of them, despite several legislative attempts. Dr. Jay Wolfson, a health policy expert at USF Health, said the insurance practice raises serious fairness concerns and called it a double dip by insurance companies. Pharmacy benefit managers and insurance companies argue a ban could drive up patient costs. A federal rule is supposed to protect patients when there is no generic equivalent for a drug, but a lack of federal guidance and enforcement means insurers are largely ignoring it. Jakafi does not have a generic equivalent.

After Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone contacted Oscar Health, Mark Armstrong received his new medication, though how, why, and who is paying for it remains unclear. A spokesperson for Oscar Health provided a statement but its contents were not detailed. Armstrong said the situation almost feels like fraud. His wife Michele said watching her husband fight for medication that was clearly working has been horrible and questioned how insurance company executives sleep at night.

cards.headline: Second arrest made in fatal shooting of Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Barnes
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that a second person has been arrested in the fatal shooting of Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Leonard Barnes, 66. Karen Moye, the victim's sister and mother of the primary suspect, has been charged with false report to law enforcement and the commission of a capital felony for knowingly providing false information to investigators and withholding pertinent information related to the homicide investigation. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said during a press conference that detectives uncovered information indicating Moye deliberately misled the investigation. Mincey, 41, Barnes' nephew, was formally charged with first-degree murder Saturday in connection with Barnes' death and remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail without bond. Deputies said the fatal shooting was premeditated.

The fatal shooting happened July 7 at a residence on the 2700 block of Essex Drive in Fort Pierce. Deputies responded to the home at around 3:30 p.m. after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned a man had shot another man with a rifle. Barnes was taken to a local hospital, where he died. Moye, who lived in the home with Mincey and Barnes, heard a loud bang while she was in the bathroom and came out to find Mincey sitting at a table with a rifle in his lap and called police, according to an arrest affidavit. During questioning, Mincey told detectives he could not recall what happened the day of the shooting and that he did not have any issues with Barnes and did not know how Barnes died, though he admitted to owning two firearms.

Moye told detectives immediately after the shooting that Mincey and Barnes did not have a good relationship and that Mincey expressed fear in the days leading up to the shooting, the arrest affidavit said. She said Mincey told her Barnes was trying to kill him and that Mincey did not want to be left alone at the house. In a follow-up interview Monday, Moye gave a detective conflicting accounts of what happened on the day of the shooting. She told detectives she was in fear of Barnes and that something might happen between Mincey and Barnes. When asked why she did not notify police, she said she thought both of them would get in trouble and that she was sorry for not providing complete information initially.

Barnes worked as an art teacher for the St. Lucie County School District since 2017, serving at West Gate K-8 and Samuel S. Gaines Academy. He leaves behind three adult children. Former student Caila Coleman, who said Barnes was her seventh-grade teacher in Tallahassee, remembered him as a pillar of the community and father figure. Del Toro said providing false information intentionally and withholding information during a homicide investigation delays justice, diverts investigative resources, and can impact the family's ability to receive answers. Deputies said the fatal shooting remains an active investigation and are encouraging anyone with information to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: Florida Democrats point to special-election wins as party seeks to break Republican supermajorities
cards.body:
Florida Democrats outlined a path Monday to break Republican supermajorities in the state Legislature, pointing to more than 30 local and special-election flips since the 2024 election as evidence that momentum is building ahead of the 2026 midterms. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said during a virtual briefing that the party has recruited more than 3,000 volunteers and holds an advantage in requests for vote-by-mail ballots. "The Republican supermajority in this legislature is breakable, and we are going to break it this cycle," Fried said. The party's tally includes local offices as well as recent legislative special elections, not 30 seats in the Florida Legislature. Fried attributed the gains to the Pendulum Project, a year-round organizing operation designed to maintain voter contact between major elections.

Democrats are building their message around affordability, blaming nearly three decades of Republican control for rising housing, property insurance, healthcare and everyday living costs. The party's candidates will also challenge a Republican-backed property-tax amendment headed to voters, arguing that cutting local government revenue could threaten services or shift costs elsewhere. "If they wanted to reduce the cost of living for everyday Floridians, they could have done that through the legislative process," Fried said. "Instead, what they're doing is making our local governments the big boogeyman." Party leaders believe dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and economic conditions could help Democrats reconnect with working-class voters, younger Floridians and voters with no party affiliation. Senate Democratic Leader-designate Tracie Davis said the party has "put in place the programs needed to capitalize and break these supermajorities once and for all."

The climb remains steep for Florida Democrats. Gov. Ron DeSantis defeated Democrat Charlie Crist by roughly 19 percentage points in 2022. Two years later, Trump carried Florida over Kamala Harris by about 13 points, the largest Republican presidential margin in the state since 1988. Republicans have built a voter registration advantage of more than 1.5 million. As of May 31, Florida had about 5.54 million active registered Republicans and 4.03 million Democrats, according to the state Division of Elections. Another 3.32 million voters were registered without a party affiliation. Republicans remain at or above the two-thirds threshold needed for supermajority power in both legislative chambers. A two-thirds majority amounts to 80 of the 120 House seats and 27 of the 40 Senate seats when every member is present.

Democrats will continue making their case at Leadership Blue, the state party's annual gathering, scheduled for July 17 through 19 at Disney's Coronado Springs Resort in Lake Buena Vista. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will deliver the keynote address at the July 18 gala. The weekend will serve as both a rally and a strategy session as Democrats try to turn scattered victories into a broader recovery.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce neighbors pack planning meeting over 17-story Causeway Cove development proposal
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Planning Board reviewed the Causeway Cove development project on Monday, a proposal that includes five high-rise buildings off Seaway Drive, with the tallest standing 17 stories and 192 feet tall. The height exceeds the city's current limit by more than four times. The project also calls for two hotels and more than 70,000 square feet of retail space.

The development qualifies under the Live Local Act, a state law passed in 2023 that allows developers to bypass height and density restrictions as long as they set aside 40% of units for affordable housing for at least 30 years. The project includes more than 900 apartments and condos, with 365 designated as affordable housing.

Neighbors packed the chamber on Monday to raise concerns about the project. Buster Brewster, a boater at Causeway Cove Marina, said he worries the project will change the character of the area. "We're going to put this big old conglomerate up here, and I'm just afraid it's going to take away from the beauty of this place," Brewster said. Dennis Fein attended the meeting and raised concerns about traffic. "Nobody's thought this out," Fein said. "You're going to have massive traffic jams. Nobody's going to be able to get on the island, off the island," Fein said. City Planning Director Kev Freeman said developers must add traffic mitigation efforts and any required intersection or access improvements.

City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city has no authority over whether the project is approved. "The city does not have a play here. We do not have a position in this. This is regulated by the state of Florida in the entirety. The city has been eliminated from the process," Broderick said. City commissioners are scheduled to hear a review of the project as the next step in the process.

cards.headline: Rising insurance costs emerging as midterm election issue for Florida voters, study finds
cards.teaser: A new study from Insurify found 65% of Florida respondents said rising insurance costs would make them more likely to vote in the 2026 midterms, higher than the national average of 58%.
cards.body:
A new study from online insurance marketplace Insurify found 58% of Americans say rising home insurance costs are making them more likely to vote in the 2026 elections. In Florida, that number climbs to 65%. Insurify economist Julia Taliesin said the company wanted to look at whether there was any connection in some of these states between the political environment and insurance regulation. Insurify puts the Florida statewide average premium at $8,292, with a modest 2% increase expected this year.

The study found 84% of Florida respondents plan to vote in the 2026 midterms, with 72% of Florida respondents being homeowners. Additionally, 49% of Florida homeowners reported their home insurance premiums increased in the last 12 months, and 71% of Florida respondents believe elections affect home insurance costs in their state. Republican state leaders this year have been leading the charge for property tax reform as a new affordability target. Taliesin said insurance complexity may be driving that political shift in focus. It demonstrates about what is easiest to shift where they can focus and get maybe the biggest result, and insurance is complicated, she said.

cards.headline: World Cup semifinals set as England and Argentina advance to final four
cards.teaser: England beat Norway behind two goals from Jude Bellingham, while Argentina defeated Switzerland in extra time to reach the World Cup semifinals.
cards.body:
England and Argentina advanced to the World Cup semifinals over the weekend, defeating Norway and Switzerland in the quarterfinals. England's Jude Bellingham scored twice to lead his team past Erling Haaland's Norway. For Argentina, Julián Alvarez scored in extra time to help the defending champion advance, with assistance from a controversial VAR call. The semifinal matchup between England and Argentina is now set, with both teams relying on key players to reach this stage. Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham have each scored six goals in the competition for England. The team was last in a World Cup semifinal in 2018 but lost to Croatia. England is searching for its first World Cup title since 1966. Argentina has scored 17 goals in the tournament, the most of any team, and many members of the current squad won the title in 2022.

The other semifinal will feature France against Spain. France has been considered the tournament favorite, with Kylian Mbappé leading the front line alongside Ousmane Dembélé. Spain has conceded just one goal the entire tournament. Spain beat France in the semifinals of Euro 2024, a tournament it won, and also defeated France in the Nations League last year. Legendary manager Didier Deschamps is leaving his role with France after this tournament. The final is scheduled for July 19.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks community support as husband battles head and neck cancer
cards.teaser: Dave and Faren Motz of Hobe Sound are asking for community support as Dave undergoes treatment for head and neck cancer, with medical costs reaching nearly $20,000 out of pocket.
cards.body:
Dave and Faren Motz met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised three children. Faren home schooled all three kids and the couple started a farm business where they served children. Just months after the couple purchased a property in Hobe Sound, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer. Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments at AdventHealth in Celebration. The repeated visits to Orlando, biopsies, scans, and exams added up, costing the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket. Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid.

AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource for the couple. Faren said kind people who gave to their charity saved her husband's life. Dave, a former firefighter, had long been the family's provider, but now Faren has stepped up to support them both. Doctors told Dave he has an 85% chance of recovery. Faren works at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort, where those who want to show their support can stop by and visit. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

cards.headline: Jannik Sinner wins second straight Wimbledon title, beats Alexander Zverev in four sets
cards.teaser: Top-ranked Jannik Sinner captured his fifth Grand Slam title and second consecutive Wimbledon championship Sunday, defeating Alexander Zverev 6-7, 7-6, 6-3, 6-4.
cards.body:
Jannik Sinner beat Alexander Zverev 6-7 (7), 7-6 (2), 6-3, 6-4 Sunday for his second consecutive title at the All England Club. The top-ranked Italian's fifth Grand Slam title came in his first tournament since a second-round meltdown at the French Open, where he wilted in a Paris heat wave. When Sinner ripped a forehand winner up the line on his first match point, he dropped to the grass on his back in celebration.

Zverev earned his first break point of the match at 3-3 in the third set, but slipped and appeared to hyper-extend his right knee as he attempted to change directions behind the baseline. Zverev grasped his knee in apparent discomfort and Sinner went around the net and helped his opponent up off the grass. Zverev quickly resumed playing but appeared slightly hampered and missed a forehand that handed Sinner the first break of the match and a 5-3 lead in the third set.

It was Sinner's 10th straight victory over Zverev, who was coming off his first Grand Slam title at the French Open. Despite the defeat in the final, Zverev will move into the No. 2 spot in the rankings on Monday. Prince William joined his wife Kate and two of their children for the final in a star-studded Royal Box that also included actors Dustin Hoffman, Nicole Kidman and Ben Stiller.

cards.headline: Czech player Linda Noskova wins Wimbledon women's title after wasting five match points
cards.teaser: Linda Noskova recovered from a second-set meltdown to defeat Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 in an all-Czech final Saturday for her first Grand Slam trophy.
cards.body:
Linda Noskova is the latest in a long line of Czech women to win Wimbledon. The 21-year-old Noskova recovered from a second-set meltdown in which she wasted five match points to overcome Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 in an all-Czech final on Saturday for her first Grand Slam trophy. Noskova became the third Czech woman in four years to win the grass-court major, after Marketa Vondrousova in 2023 and Barbora Krejcikova in 2024.

Petra Kvitova, who won Wimbledon in 2011 and 2014, was in attendance, as was Martina Navratilova, who won a record nine singles titles at the All England Club. Navratilova looked on from the Royal Box, where she was seated next to Kate, the Princess of Wales, who was due to present the Venus Rosewater Dish trophy to Noskova. Muchova and Noskova played doubles together at the 2024 Paris Olympics and finished fourth. In the men's final on Sunday, top-ranked Jannik Sinner will attempt to defend his title against French Open champion Alexander Zverev.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie soccer stadium groundbreaking set for November, new renderings show 6,000-seat venue at Walton Road site
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie SC released new renderings this week of its 6,000-seat soccer stadium and announced Friday that groundbreaking is anticipated in November. The stadium will be built at the Walton & One development, a 46-acre mixed-use redevelopment project located along U.S. 1 and Walton Road. The club's inaugural season begins in 2027, but the stadium is scheduled to open in early 2028. The team has not announced where they plan to play next year while the facility is under construction. The club posted Thursday on social media that their home venue will be "a place where soccer, community, and unforgettable moments will come together." Ticket deposits are currently available online.

The club said the 6,000-seat venue will have flexibility to grow in capacity and described it as a year-round gathering place. The club said on X that every space has been designed to create unforgettable experiences, from matchdays to concerts, festivals, and community events. Port St. Lucie resident Zach Woods said this may be the first cool thing the city has brought to the area, though he expressed concern that additional traffic on U.S. 1 on gamedays will be huge. Focus Sanders, a barber at Sapp's Barbershop, said the stadium offers more business because it will bring more people to the area, including visitors from out of town. The city was awarded a United Soccer League League One Team last October when Port St. Lucie city council members unanimously approved both the funding and operating agreements. The city said the stadium is an $80 million economic investment, and no taxpayer money will be used for construction. Diego Delledonne, the club's chief operating officer, released a statement Friday.

As the 2026 midterm elections approach, the cost of homeowners insurance is becoming a key political issue, according to a new study from online insurance marketplace Insurify. The study found 58% of Americans say rising home insurance costs are making them more likely to vote in the 2026 elections. In Florida, that number climbs to 65%. Insurify puts the Florida statewide average premium at $8,292, with a modest 2% increase expected this year. The study found 84% of Florida respondents plan to vote in the 2026 midterms and 72% of Florida respondents are homeowners. Among Florida homeowners, 49% reported their home insurance premiums increased in the last 12 months. The study also found 57% of Florida respondents feel negative about the state of the economy and 71% of Florida respondents believe elections affect home insurance costs in their state.

According to state leaders, reforms on insurance litigation have led to stable and in many cases lower rates, as more companies enter Florida adding to competition. Yet in many parts of the state, including South Florida, insurance premiums have risen as inflation and home values have increased. Republican state leaders this year have been leading the charge for property tax reform as a new affordability target. Insurify economist Julia Taliesin said insurance complexity may be driving that political shift in focus.

hero.headline: Martin County faces $2.1 billion transportation funding gap with nine road widening projects unfunded
hero.teaser: Martin County will need approximately $2.8 billion for transportation improvements over the next 20 years but only $701 million is currently available, leaving nine identified road widening projects without funding.
hero.body:
Martin County faces a $2.1 billion transportation funding shortfall over the next two decades, with nine road widening projects left without financial backing, according to a PowerPoint obtained through a public records request. The Martin County Metropolitan Planning Organization estimates the county will need approximately $2.8 billion for transportation improvements over the next 20 years, but only $701 million is currently available. This means the county can fund just about one quarter of its identified transportation needs.

Beth Beltran, administrator for Martin County's Metropolitan Planning Organization, said the cost analysis was emailed to county and Stuart officials last August. Of the $701 million currently available, all but $10 million comes from state and federal funding sources. The significant funding gap has forced difficult decisions about which transportation projects can move forward and which must remain on hold.

Among the most pressing unfunded needs are nine roads the county identified as requiring widening as traffic grows. The total cost to widen those roads is approximately $213 million, money that is not currently available, leaving all nine projects out of the county's draft Cost Feasible Plan. Those roads include SW Martin Downs Boulevard, SR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW 96th Street, SW Bridge Road, CR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW Allapattah Road/CR-609, SE Green River Parkway, SW Indiantown Avenue, and SE Bridge Road/CR-708.

State Road 710 is among the county's highest priorities due to safety concerns. Beltran said fatal crashes as well as serious injury crashes were just enormous on that corridor, with improvements estimated at about $300 million. The substantial price tag for State Road 710 alone represents nearly half of the total funding shortfall and highlights the challenge facing county officials as they balance safety needs against available resources. The funding gap affects not just road widening projects but a range of transportation improvements needed across the county over the next two decades.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie couple opposes rezoning of lot behind their home from residential to commercial
hero.teaser: Joseph and Margaret Mucciolo say the Port St. Lucie City Council approved rezoning the lot behind their yard where trees currently stand, despite their months-long opposition.
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie couple is searching for answers after the city council voted unanimously to rezone the lot behind their home from residential to commercial, despite their months-long opposition. Joseph and Margaret Mucciolo say their backyard views of nature and sense of quiet relaxation that drew them to purchase the property are now under threat. Margaret Mucciolo told reporters she saw the beautiful setting and told the real estate agent to get ready to make an offer because it just felt like home. Joseph Mucciolo said that in six months or a year, the trees currently standing behind their yard are going to be gone.

The Port St. Lucie City Council approved changing the lot behind their yard where trees currently stand to be rezoned from residential to commercial. The council says the change is necessary to reduce traffic in the neighborhood. One council member explained that adding commercial closer to neighborhoods reduces the length of trips, which reduces overall traffic because if you have commercial closer to you, your trips are shorter and it reduces the burden on the overall network. The Mucciolos have fought the rezoning for months and feel their voices have gone unheard throughout the process.

The couple spoke at Monday's meeting voicing their concerns, but they feel the council left them unheard, leaving them searching for answers about where to go from here. Joseph Mucciolo questioned whether they can make an objection and have this looked at again. The council held its second reading Monday, and while there was public comment, it was what's called a quasi-judicial hearing. This means council members act as a panel of judges applying existing zoning rules to a specific property and making decisions based strictly on sworn testimony and factual evidence, not public opinion.

Margaret Mucciolo said the process needs to change until it's logical, transparent, caring, and provides hope for people. She emphasized that this is her home and expressed frustration with feeling ignored except by the news media. The couple says they will be exploring any kind of appeal process to change this outcome or to change the next one. Their fight represents a broader concern about how rezoning decisions impact longtime residents who purchased their homes based on the existing character of their neighborhoods.

cards.headline: Second arrest made in Fort Pierce art teacher's fatal shooting on Essex Drive
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced a second arrest in the fatal shooting of Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, who died July 7 at a residence on the 2700 block of Essex Drive. Karen Moye, identified as the victim's sister and mother of the suspect, faces charges of false report to law enforcement and commission of a capital felony for knowingly providing false information to investigators and withholding pertinent information related to the homicide investigation, Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Tuesday during a press conference. Christopher Mincey, 41, Barnes' nephew, was formally charged with first-degree murder Saturday in connection with Barnes' death and remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail without bond. Deputies responded to the home around 3:30 p.m. after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. Moye heard a loud bang while in the bathroom and came out to find Mincey sitting at a table with a rifle in his lap and called police, an arrest affidavit said. Barnes was taken to a local hospital, where he died.

Moye, who lived in the home with Mincey and Barnes, told detectives immediately after the shooting that the pair did not have a good relationship and that Mincey expressed fear in the days leading up to the shooting, saying Barnes was trying to kill him and he did not want to be left alone at the house, the arrest affidavit said. In a follow-up interview Monday, Moye gave a detective conflicting accounts of what happened and said she was in fear of Barnes and thought something might happen between Mincey and Barnes. When asked why she didn't notify police, she said she thought both of them would get in trouble and was sorry for not providing complete information initially. Barnes worked as an art teacher for the St. Lucie County School District since 2017, serving at West Gate K-8 and Samuel S. Gaines Academy, and leaves behind three adult children. Former student Caila Coleman, who said Barnes was her seventh-grade teacher in Tallahassee, remembered him as a pillar of the community and father figure.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Opens Registration for Free City University Program
cards.teaser:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes
cards.body:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes begin Wednesday, Aug. 12, and will be held from **5:30 to 8:30 p.m. in the Council Chambers at Port St. Lucie City Hall**, located at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

Participants will learn about City departments, municipal services and the decision-making processes that shape the community. The program also gives residents opportunities to meet City staff, ask questions and gain a closer look at the work involved in operating one of Florida's largest cities.

Residents who complete the course will receive a certificate of completion and may also choose to become a City Ambassador, helping share information about City programs and services throughout the community.

City University is intended to encourage civic engagement while strengthening connections between residents and local government. Since the program began in 2016, more than 600 residents have participated.

**Enrollment is limited to 160 participants.**

Residents who are unable to attend the in-person classes can also access City U on Demand, which offers a more flexible way to learn about Port St. Lucie government and municipal operations.

hero.headline: Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse offers 165 years of history with 105-step climb to panoramic views
hero.teaser: The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, built in 1860, offers visitors a 105-step climb to panoramic views of the Atlantic Ocean, Jupiter Inlet, and Loxahatchee and Indian rivers.
hero.body:
The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, a red brick tower constructed in 1860 at the base of the Jupiter Inlet on Florida's Atlantic coast, has operated continuously for 165 years as both an active navigational aid and a public attraction. The historic structure has guided mariners since before the Civil War while welcoming visitors who climb to its observation gallery for sweeping views of the surrounding waterways and coastline. The lighthouse's design allows modern visitors to follow the same path that lighthouse keepers took throughout history to maintain operations.

Reaching the observation gallery at the top requires ascending 105 steps up a narrow spiral staircase that winds through the interior of the brick tower. This route follows the same path that lighthouse keepers climbed night after night to maintain the powerful Fresnel lens that projected light across the water to passing ships. The spiral staircase leads upward through the tower to the gallery at the top, allowing modern visitors to retrace the steps of the early keepers who ensured the beacon remained operational throughout the decades.

The observation gallery provides panoramic views stretching across multiple waterways and the ocean. The Atlantic Ocean extends to the east, while below the tower, the turquoise waters of the Jupiter Inlet converge with the Loxahatchee and Indian rivers. Visitors at this elevated vantage point can watch boats glide through the channel as sea breezes sweep across the observation area. The commanding perspective reveals why this location proved ideal for a lighthouse, offering clear sightlines across the coastal landscape and waterways that allowed keepers to monitor maritime traffic and project the beacon across miles of ocean.

The museum grounds preserve more than just the tower itself. Restored historic buildings chronicle the lighthouse's journey from its construction before the Civil War through its years as an active Coast Guard station. These structures provide information about the lighthouse's role in regional maritime history and offer details about the daily lives of the keepers who operated the station. The site maintains the supporting buildings that allowed the lighthouse station to function across more than a century and a half of continuous service, preserving the complete story of this working navigational aid that has marked the Florida coastline for generations of mariners.
